video_title: Rekordhøy kroneavkastning | Resultatfremleggelsen for første halvår 2026
gist: Norway's NOK 22,683bn sovereign wealth fund reported its largest-ever half-year krone return, NOK 1,753bn or 9.4%, with more than NOK 1,000bn of it from technology alone and semiconductor names dominating the contributors. Management flagged record concentration (top 10 holdings above 20% of the index, technology near a third of the US market, the US at almost 55% of the fund), an explicit 40% drawdown scenario led by a break in AI optimism, and a broad erosion of shareholder rights visible in the SpaceX listing and in US companies reincorporating in Texas.

insights.claim: Norway's sovereign wealth fund ended H1 2026 at NOK 22,683bn, the highest quarter-end value in its history, after a 9.4% return.
insights.speaker: Trond Grande (NBIM deputy CEO)
insights.so_what: The world's largest single equity owner is at peak AUM with 70% in global stocks, so any forced rebalancing or mandate change becomes a globally material flow.
insights.quote: And this number here, 22,683 billion kroner, is the highest number ever at the end of a quarter.

insights.claim: The fund posted its largest-ever half-year krone return at NOK 1,753bn, while a stronger Norwegian krone subtracted roughly NOK 400bn and inflows added about NOK 100bn.
insights.speaker: Trond Grande (NBIM deputy CEO)
insights.so_what: Krone strength is a NOK 400bn-per-half-year swing factor, so headline fund figures reported in kroner are a poor read on underlying asset performance.
insights.quote: The first half of the year was the highest krone return this fund has ever had, with 1,753 billion kroner.

insights.claim: Equities returned 13% in H1 2026 with more than NOK 1,000bn of that coming from technology alone, and every sector was positive except consumer discretionary.
insights.speaker: Trond Grande (NBIM deputy CEO)
insights.so_what: Well over half the fund's record half-year came from one sector, quantifying how single-factor global equity returns have become.
insights.quote: It is mainly technology, where there is more than 1,000 billion coming from technology, but basically all the industries have developed positively in a way with the exception of consumer discretionary.

insights.claim: The fund's roughly 1,000-property real estate portfolio returned about 3% in H1 2026, two points of it from rental income, the first positive stretch in a long time after three years of underperforming the equity benchmark it is measured against.
insights.speaker: Trond Grande (NBIM deputy CEO)
insights.so_what: Global institutional real estate is inflecting from write-downs back to income-plus-modest-revaluation, an early signal for listed property valuations.
insights.quote: We have almost 1,000 properties all over the world. Well, here we now had positive development and we haven't seen that in a long time.

insights.claim: The ten largest companies now make up more than 20% of the fund's equity index and technology is close to a third of the US stock index, a level never previously reached.
insights.speaker: Trond Grande (NBIM deputy CEO)
insights.so_what: An index-replicating owner of 7,000 companies is now structurally forced into the most concentrated global equity market on record.
insights.quote: the 10 largest companies are more than 20% and also that technology, uh, technology companies are almost a third of the stock index in America. And it has never been this high before.

insights.claim: The top contributors to the fund's technology return were dominated almost entirely by semiconductor names, an unprecedented degree of single-industry concentration in the return drivers.
insights.speaker: Trond Grande (NBIM deputy CEO)
insights.so_what: Return breadth has collapsed to one supply chain: chip-cycle risk is now effectively market risk for a global index investor.
insights.quote: It's chips chips chips chips chips chips not chips chips chips chips. So we've probably never seen such concentration before.

insights.claim: H1 2026 sector leadership was driven by Asian technology companies rather than US megacaps, with the Korean index cited as exceptionally strong and new, simpler chip types leading hardware rather than the chips that led the previous leg up.
insights.speaker: Trond Grande (NBIM deputy CEO)
insights.so_what: Leadership has rotated to Asian tech and down the silicon complexity curve, arguing against assuming the same US names keep leading.
insights.quote: it's particularly driven by the Asian technology companies. For example, in Korea the index has been very very eh strong.

insights.claim: Companies selling simple software that AI can replace have already seen their share prices fall, and NBIM itself is now replacing bought software with tools it builds in-house.
insights.speaker: Trond Grande (NBIM deputy CEO)
insights.so_what: A large institutional software buyer describing itself cutting vendors is customer-side confirmation of AI seat-cannibalisation and a leading indicator for SaaS revenue.
insights.quote: we can now replace our software with things that we have developed ourselves

insights.claim: The US now accounts for almost 55% of the fund and a Ministry of Finance committee is reviewing both geographic spread and concentration risk, against a track record where US earnings growth and market performance over the last decade were roughly twice Europe's.
insights.speaker: Nicolai Tangen (NBIM CEO)
insights.so_what: Any mandated cut to the US weight of a fund this size is a slow mechanical multi-year outflow from US equities, and the committee must justify giving up a documented 2x earnings-growth differential.
insights.quote: over the last 10 years the earnings growth in the US and performance in the stock market has been twice that of Europe

insights.claim: As a near-index-replicating fund, NBIM says it can do very little about concentration risk itself - any fix must come through a change to the Ministry of Finance benchmark.
insights.speaker: Nicolai Tangen (NBIM CEO)
insights.so_what: Signals the largest holder of global equities will not de-concentrate voluntarily, so index concentration persists until a political process changes the benchmark.
insights.quote: This means that the way we have invested is close to the index or the trading list that we receive from the Ministry of Finance. So there is a limit to what we can do with that concentration risk.

themes.theme: SpaceX IPO and the pre-IPO AI cohort

insights.claim: NBIM held NOK 12bn in SpaceX at end-H1 2026 after the IPO, equal to roughly 1% of the 5% free float and only about 0.05% of the whole company, and stayed roughly index weight through the summer despite a sharp decline in the shares.
insights.speaker: Nicolai Tangen (NBIM CEO)
insights.so_what: Shows how little of these mega-valuations index money can own while float stays tiny - scarcity, not institutional demand, sets the price - and that no large sovereign bid stepped into the post-IPO drawdown.
insights.quote: So then our ownership stake in Space 6 is 0.05%.

insights.claim: OpenAI and Anthropic are named alongside SpaceX as the AI-optimism listings expected to bring progressively more of their equity into freely traded public markets.
insights.speaker: Trond Grande (NBIM deputy CEO)
insights.so_what: Index funds become mechanically forced buyers as these floats grow, so float expansion schedules are the tradeable variable in the next AI listings.
insights.quote: And then it is expected that more and more of the companies will, er, come and become freely traded, right?

insights.claim: NBIM participates in up to 400 IPOs a year through a dedicated equity capital markets desk and applied that same standard process to SpaceX.
insights.speaker: Nicolai Tangen (NBIM CEO)
insights.so_what: A 400-IPO-a-year cornerstone buyer is a structural bid in primary markets and its ECM process functions as a de facto governance screen for issuers.
insights.quote: So we take up to 400 IPOs per year in new companies which are coming to the stock exchange and we have a separate department which is coordinating that process.

insights.claim: Tangen identifies the SpaceX IPO's distinguishing feature as its diminished shareholder rights via share classes with different voting power, not its business or valuation.
insights.speaker: Nicolai Tangen (NBIM CEO)
insights.so_what: The largest index owner is publicly flagging governance, not fundamentals, as the price of admission to the new mega-IPOs - a template other issuers will copy.
insights.quote: the eh the shareholder rights associated with that IPO was different as we all know and I would say that's the that's the difference

themes.theme: Shareholder rights erosion and the Texas migration

insights.claim: Shareholder rights are being weakened across many markets simultaneously through new dual share classes, fewer rights to sue companies and reduced reporting requirements, which NBIM says worries it even though it supports removing unnecessary regulation.
insights.speaker: Carine (NBIM responsible-investment lead)
insights.so_what: Minority-investor protection is deteriorating structurally, raising the governance discount warranted on newly listed and reincorporated companies.
insights.quote: Typical changes are that we get fewer voting rights because different share classes with different voting rights are created. There are fewer opportunities to sue companies and there are fewer reporting requirements from companies.

insights.claim: US state-level competition for incorporations - notably companies relocating headquarters to Texas where shareholder rights are weaker - became a new proxy-voting topic this season, with NBIM supporting ExxonMobil's move but voting against Archer Aviation's.
insights.speaker: Carine (NBIM responsible-investment lead)
insights.so_what: Reincorporation votes are now a live governance risk factor and NBIM's case-by-case standard is a published screen other investors can mirror.
insights.quote: It was that there were many companies in the United States that wanted to move their headquarters to Texas, where shareholder rights are weaker and the companies have more power.

insights.claim: Sustainability shareholder proposals have halved over the last two years and NBIM is voting for fewer of them, attributing this to declining proposal quality rather than reduced commitment.
insights.speaker: Carine (NBIM responsible-investment lead)
insights.so_what: The most systematic large ESG voter - roughly 76,000 proposals across 7,000 companies this half year - is quietly reducing support, marking the fading of the ESG-resolution channel of corporate pressure.
insights.quote: we are seeing fewer of these, it has actually halved in the last two years. And we also vote less eh for these shareholder proposals on sustainability.

insights.claim: NBIM held about 200 company meetings on climate in the half year and voted in favour of a shareholder proposal at Nvidia demanding better reporting of its climate emissions.
insights.speaker: Carine (NBIM responsible-investment lead)
insights.so_what: Datacentre and supply-chain emissions disclosure is becoming a governance pressure point at the single most important AI supplier.
insights.quote: we, among other things, voted in favor of a shareholder proposal at the chip company, Nvidia, that they should be better at reporting on their climate emissions

insights.claim: While an ethics-guidelines committee is working, the fund cannot add new exclusions or observations but can reverse existing ones, and has already readmitted previously excluded shipbreaking companies that changed their practices.
insights.speaker: Carine (NBIM responsible-investment lead)
insights.so_what: Exclusion flow is asymmetric right now - only re-inclusions are possible - so previously excluded names can get a mechanical NBIM bid with no mandate change.
insights.quote: we can't exclude any new companies , but we can remove the exclusion from, that is, remove the exclusion.

themes.theme: Renewables build-out and the blocked private-equity mandate

insights.claim: NBIM has invested roughly NOK 140bn gross in renewable infrastructure against a 2% cap that would currently allow around NOK 400bn, and intends to keep building the portfolio.
insights.speaker: Trond Grande (NBIM deputy CEO)
insights.so_what: Roughly NOK 260bn of unused headroom at a single buyer makes NBIM a persistent bid for large-scale renewable projects.
insights.quote: So we have invested approximately 140 billion kroner on a gross basis, a little less on a net basis. Eh, but we imagine that will increase.

insights.claim: The fund deliberately went slow on renewables after getting the mandate in 2021 because prices were bid up by heavy competition, and accelerated only once higher interest rates thinned out rival bidders and improved return prospects.
insights.speaker: Trond Grande (NBIM deputy CEO)
insights.so_what: A large patient buyer publicly timing entry to the post-rate-shock repricing of infrastructure signals that renewable project returns have genuinely reset higher.
insights.quote: And then interest rates have risen and the competition for the projects that we are looking at, which are very large projects, is not as tough as it was. So now we see much better return opportunities

insights.claim: Renewable infrastructure is held for diversification because its returns are driven by power prices and are largely uncorrelated with equities in the short term, and the fund's renewable assets now generate power equal to about 10% of all Norwegian energy production despite a 0% return in H1 2026.
insights.speaker: Trond Grande (NBIM deputy CEO)
insights.so_what: Frames renewables as a power-price-linked, equity-uncorrelated income stream rather than a green allocation - the argument other pension funds will reuse - and makes the fund a utility-scale generator exposed to European power volatility.
insights.quote: So it does n't fluctuate in line with many of the other risks that we have in it, which are primarily energy prices and electricity or power, eh, and it's not that correlated with stock prices, at least in the short term.

insights.claim: NBIM's long-standing request for a private equity mandate remains rejected by the Ministry of Finance, with no new development since the last refusal roughly half a year ago.
insights.speaker: Nicolai Tangen (NBIM CEO)
insights.so_what: The single largest potential new LP for global private equity stays sidelined for political rather than valuation reasons.
insights.quote: it is a well-known fact that the fund has wanted to invest in private equity for a long period of time and has also proposed it to the ministry. Eh, and then they came back and said that it was not applicable at that time.

themes.theme: The 40% drawdown scenario and the crash-buyer commitment

insights.claim: NBIM's published scenario work says the fund could fall as much as 40% under not-unrealistic assumptions - a break in AI optimism, further geopolitical fragmentation, a debt-repayment confidence shock, extreme climate events, or several at once.
insights.speaker: Trond Grande (NBIM deputy CEO)
insights.so_what: The world's largest equity owner publicly sizes its tail risk at 40% and names a break in AI optimism as the leading trigger - a usable institutional stress-test benchmark.
insights.quote: then the fund could fall quite dramatically in value with not too unrealistic assumptions so up to maybe 40% eh fall in the fund value we have to be mentally prepared for

insights.claim: Tangen argues the last 30 years of abnormally strong financial markets cannot continue, on the historical ground that no financial fortune has ever persisted.
insights.speaker: Nicolai Tangen (NBIM CEO)
insights.so_what: The custodian of a record-value portfolio is explicitly guiding down forward return expectations at the peak - a top-of-cycle sentiment marker.
insights.quote: And the reason for that is that no financial fortune has ever persisted. Everything has always disappeared in the end.

insights.claim: A built-in rebalancing rule commits the fund to buying more equities and selling bonds to fund it whenever stocks fall sharply, as it did through the financial crisis, and management says it will sit through a drawdown rather than de-risk.
insights.speaker: Nicolai Tangen (NBIM CEO)
insights.so_what: A mechanical, politically insulated buyer of global equities in a crash - and a simultaneous seller of bonds, which matters for crisis bond liquidity.
insights.quote: there's a rebalancing rule built into what we do that says that if the shares go down a lot, we buy, we buy more, and then we sell bonds to finance it

insights.claim: Tangen says the fund's mandate is anchored broadly enough across the Storting that NBIM does not expect political interference or forced selling during a market decline, citing the fund's behaviour in the financial crisis.
insights.speaker: Nicolai Tangen (NBIM CEO)
insights.so_what: Political durability is the fund's real edge and makes it one of the few pools of capital structurally able to buy into a crash rather than sell it.
insights.quote: I think that one of the nice things about the Norwegian model is that it is so strongly anchored in the Storting, that is, quite broadly politically, so that we do not expect any change in our mandate

insights.claim: Economic and market outcomes in 2026 have massively exceeded what was forecast two years earlier despite trade and tariff barriers and an energy crisis, and technology and AI are credited as the main reason.
insights.speaker: Trond Grande (NBIM deputy CEO)
insights.so_what: Attributing the entire resilience surprise to AI is exactly why a break in AI optimism is the fund's number-one tail scenario - the upside and the tail share one driver.
insights.quote: it is actually quite incredible that the development has been so strong. And a lot of the reason it has been that way is because of what's happening in technology and in AI.

themes.theme: China pharma and AI in drug discovery

insights.claim: Tangen says pharmaceutical sector leaders expect China to be ahead of Europe in cancer research within two years, helped by stronger innovation and patent output, faster clinical trials and far less regulatory red tape.
insights.speaker: Nicolai Tangen (NBIM CEO)
insights.so_what: A two-year horizon for Chinese oncology leadership reframes the licensing and M&A premium on Chinese biotech assets versus European pipelines.
insights.quote: They believe that even within cancer research, China will be further ahead than Europe in two years' time.

insights.claim: European and American pharmaceutical companies are increasingly acquiring small Chinese biotechs specifically to obtain their technology.
insights.speaker: Nicolai Tangen (NBIM CEO)
insights.so_what: Points to sustained cross-border M&A demand for Chinese small-cap biotech as the cheapest route to a competitive pipeline.
insights.quote: And we see European companies and American companies increasingly buying up Chinese small companies to get their hands on the technology.

insights.claim: Healthcare is where Tangen sees the strongest real-world results from AI so far, across research, development, new molecule discovery and genetics.
insights.speaker: Nicolai Tangen (NBIM CEO)
insights.so_what: Identifies pharma R&D rather than enterprise software as the first sector producing measurable AI output gains - where the productivity trade actually lands.
insights.quote: it is perhaps the area where we see the most, uh, results, best results from AI, both in uh, research, uh, development, new molecules
